biggestGap: A capture is ORDERED on one clock and DRAWN on another, so the order the code guarantees is not the order on screen. choreography's beats run on world.time, which main.ts advances by min(0.05, dt) — while pieces/motion.ts's play curves run on world.realTime. The two are identical at 20 fps and above and diverge below it, and interactive.ts's wall-clock backstop floors the ratio at Math.max(0.08, sceneRate), so the worst case is a fixed 12.5x + 1.5 s stretch of every beat while the travel itself keeps running at 1x. Measured on the live build at 0.32 fps by wrapping walkTo/strike/shatter: in Rxa8 the rook's approach promise resolved at real 64.931 and it did not swing until real 88.063 — 23.13 real seconds of a stone rook standing motionless beside its victim against a designed POISE of 0.16 s (145x), and 38.23 s for a move the plan prices at 3.31 s (11.5x). Worse, the travel is now SHORTER than a frame: in dxe5 the pawn's walkTo(3.392,3.392) was ordered at wall 0.030 and its 0.40 s + 0.42 s settle had both expired by the next frame 3.066 s later, so not one frame of approach was ever rasterised. The pawn is drawn at (2.978,3.029) — d4 — in EVERY frame up to and including the one in which the victim shattered 3.312 m (1.409 squares) away, and appears on e5 only 7.08 real s AFTER the destruction. The engine's own reply in the same run is the player's original sentence verbatim: black-rook-07-74 struck white-rook-00-70 from (0.032,7.014) with a gap of 16.502 m — a8 to a1, seven squares — and the white rook shattered in that frame with its killer still standing on the far rank. Under it sits a frame-rate-INDEPENDENT residue: STANDOFF is 0.86 and NEGLIGIBLE is 0.15, so an orthogonally adjacent capture needs 1.00-0.86 = 0.14 squares of approach, misses the threshold by 0.01 square (2.4 cm), and planMove returns approach=[] with station = the attacker's own square. Measured: Rxa2 logged no walkTo before the strike, a gap of 2.222 m at strike:call and the identical 2.222 m at SHATTER. That one is what the code does at 60 fps too.
critiqueDetail:
THE GUARANTEE HOLDS. king-surrender --t=2.8 returns md5 45ebe28f78b6837bb2816b5fcccbe9ab at 2,264,723 bytes, the hash and byte count of rounds 3-6. wide-establishing --t=3 captured twice is cmp-clean byte-identical, md5 f64e1f7eee0c9fa66f15630a3334c5f8 at 2,630,788 bytes. verify-mate is 3/3 with legalReplies=0 on all three lines. This round is a read-only critique; nothing in the tree was touched.

Q2 - I WATCHED A CAPTURE FRAME BY FRAME, AND THE ANSWER IS SPLIT. The renderer on this box is 0.32-0.38 fps (2.6-3.1 s per frame at 520x320 on the low tier, load average 13 from other agents), so a 0.82 s strike is sub-frame and pixels alone cannot resolve it. I therefore wrapped every PieceInstance.walkTo, every PieceInstance.strike and destruction.shatter and timestamped them on BOTH clocks, and sampled every rendered frame alongside.

IN THE CODE'S OWN CLOCKS THE ORDER IS CORRECT AND THE ROUND'S CLAIM IS TRUE. Rxa8, seven squares, clicked through the canvas: CLICK-DEST wall 0.000 -> walkTo:call wall 0.004 to (0, 6.14) for 1.55 s, i.e. to the fractional standoff 0.86 short of a8, not onto it -> walkTo:done wall 8.064 with the rook rendered at rank 6.160 -> strike:call wall 23.332 with the rook 1.913 m (0.814 squares) from the victim -> strike:CONTACT wall 26.823 carrying vicDestroyed:FALSE, so the victim was demonstrably WHOLE at the instant of the blow -> SHATTER wall 26.824, ONE MILLISECOND later, with the attacker still at rank 6.160 and 1.913 m away -> walkTo:call to (0,7) and the rook standing on a8 by wall 25.760-30.976. Travel, arrive adjacent, strike, contact, shatter, step in. Nothing is destroyed before the attacker gets there, and the blow is not delivered from a1.

ON SCREEN IT IS NOT. The strike beat is scheduled on world.time (or its wall-clock backstop) while the walk runs on world.realTime, and at 0.32 fps those two are ~60x apart. The consequence in the rook capture is a 23.13-second dead hold between arriving and swinging. The consequence in the pawn capture is worse: dxe5's approach is 0.554 squares priced at chargeSeconds -> 0.40 s, plus a 0.42 s settle, and BOTH expired between two frames. The frame table is six rows and the attacker is at (2.978,3.029) — d4 — in rows 0, 1 and 2, the victim is WHOLE in row 0 and DESTROYED in row 1, and the pawn is first drawn on e5 in row 3, 7.08 real seconds after the debris appeared. A player watching that sees a pawn on d4, a pawn on e5 blowing apart, and then the pawn on e5. That is the reported bug, still visible, arrived at by a different route. The engine's reply in the same run is the original complaint word for word: black-rook-07-74 called strike from (0.032,7.014) on a victim at (-0.010,-0.008) with gap 16.502 m, and white-rook-00-70 shattered on a1 while the black rook was still standing on a8.

AND ONE CASE FAILS AT ANY FRAME RATE. STANDOFF 0.86 vs NEGLIGIBLE 0.15: an orthogonally adjacent capture has 1.00 - 0.86 = 0.14 squares of approach, 0.01 square (2.4 cm) under the threshold, so planMove drops the approach entirely and sets station to the attacker's own square. Measured on Rxa2: no walkTo before the strike at all, strike:call gap 2.222 m, SHATTER gap the identical 2.222 m, attacker at (0.027,0.031) both times. The file's own note says 'any further and the blade lands in air' about 0.86; this delivers from 1.00. Rook-takes-rook and queen-takes-pawn on an adjacent square are not rare.

Q3 - TRAVEL SCALES WITH DISTANCE, BUT ONLY TO 5.17 SQUARES. chargeSeconds is clamp(units x 0.36, 0.40, 1.55), so the ceiling binds at 4.31 squares of travel = 5.17 squares of separation and every capture longer than that walks for exactly 1.55 s. Bundling choreography.ts and pricing a1xa[n]: 1 sq -> 0.000 s of travel (below NEGLIGIBLE), 2 -> 0.410, 3 -> 0.770, 4 -> 1.130, 5 -> 1.490, 6 -> 1.550, 7 -> 1.550. Mean speed therefore RISES with distance: 6.53 m/s at 2-5 squares, 7.79 at six, 9.31 at seven. The pawn's d4xe5 charge is 1.30 m in 0.40 s = 3.26 m/s; the rook's a1xa8 charge is 14.43 m in 1.55 s = 9.31 m/s. So the long one takes 3.9x as long for 11.1x the distance and moves 2.9x faster while doing it. Whole moves: 2.16 s for the pawn against 3.31 s for the rook by the plan; 28.26 s against 38.23 s measured wall-clock on this box. The long capture is meaningfully longer. It is also, uniquely, the one that looks like a charge because the clamp makes it one.

Q4 - THE ENVELOPE IS SMOOTH; THE CARRIER IS NOT. playWalk is a pure function of time, so I evaluated the shipped curve at 4,000 samples with the real spec motion.ts builds (shoves = max(2, round(dist/0.62)), baseHalf 0.5, turnIn 0.20, turnOut 0.30, settle 0.42). It genuinely eases out of and into rest: speed at t=0+ is 1.87e-8 m/s and at arrival 4.74e-6 m/s, acceleration ramps over the first 30% and last 28% of the trip with smootherstep, and playAccel is 0 at both ends, peaks 0.933 at p=0.15 and -0.990 at p=0.85 with a flat zero cruise. No snap. But GRIND is 0.52 and velocity is envelope x (1 - 0.52 cos phi), a 3.17x peak-to-trough ripple in EVERY walk in the game, at a frequency of shoves/duration. The rook's charge is 23 shoves in 1.55 s = 14.84 shoves/s, which is 4.0 frames per shove cycle at 60 fps: sampled at 60 Hz its speed reads 18.6, 9.4, 11.9, 18.2, 8.4, 13.4, 17.4, 7.8, 15.0 m/s on consecutive frames, a 2.4x change between neighbours, peaking at 19.93 m/s — 71.7 km/h for a 3.07 m carved rook. The quiet e2-e4 push is gentler at 9.41 shoves/s (6.4 frames per cycle) and the pawn's capture charge gentlest at 5.00 (12.0 frames). FACING IS IMPLEMENTED and correct in the curve — face interpolates yaw0 -> travel heading over turnIn and back to yawRest over turnOut during the settle (verified: 0 deg -> 90 deg by t=0.35, back to 0 deg by t=1.925 on a 90-degree turn) — but I could not observe a single frame of it live, because on this box no frame of travel is ever rasterised: group.rotation.y was constant at -0.092, 0.049 and -0.012 rad through every rendered frame of the three captures.

Q5 - PACED FOR A PERSON ON THE DESIGN'S ARITHMETIC, NOT ON A SLOW RENDERER. Click to board-updated is the one number that is frame-rate free and it is excellent: 0.36-0.49 s across sixteen clicked moves (8 from the start position, 8 from an Italian). Click to the engine's answer landing in the FEN, measured over the capture-rich game: 1.46, 35.44, 3.05, 1.81, 1.83, 3.28, 3.01, 2.63 s — median 3.01 s, six of eight under four seconds, and the single 35.44 s outlier is Bxf7+, the move whose animUntilReal is longest and therefore the one the beat backstop stretches most. Click to the attacker actually standing on its destination: 38.23 s (Rxa8), 28.26 s (dxe5), 23.59 s (Rxa2). The design's own arithmetic at 20 fps or better is sound — the longest capture the module choreographs is 3.31 s and MAX_SETTLE_MS caps the reply hold at 2.2 s, so 5.5 s, inside the six-second target — but below 20 fps the backstop replaces it with 12.5 x 3.31 + 1.5 = 42.9 s and the two moves start overlapping: in the Rxa8 run the black king's reply walkTo was ordered at wall 23.331, the same frame as my rook's strike:call at 23.332.

Q6 - SIXTEEN MOVES CLICKED THROUGH THE CANVAS, EVERY POSITION LEGAL, NOTHING BROKE. Run A from the start position: e4, Bc4, Bxf7+, Qh5, Nf3, Nc3, Kf1, d4 — 16 plies, 1 capture. Run B from an Italian (r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2N2N2/PPPP1PPP/R1BQK2R w KQkq -): Nxe5, Bxf7+, Qh5, d4, O-O, bxc3, Bg5, Rc1 — 16 plies, 3 captures, including castling and a recapture. Every FEN pair from both runs was replayed through a FRESH engine bundled straight out of src/chess: ALL 32 PLIES REACHABLE BY A LEGAL MOVE, zero illegal transitions, 0 page errors and 0 console errors across both games. Add the three forced captures from the timing harness (Rxa8, dxe5 with Rxa1 in reply, Rxa2) and every capture geometry the choreographer has a branch for was exercised.

ONE SMALLER THING, MEASURED. game/index.ts clearBoard() only sets p.group.visible = false and never removes the instance from pieces/index.ts's `live` array, so pieces.all() keeps returning every man from every position the board has ever held. Three setPosition calls in one session left serials 0-31, 64-69, 70-75 and 76-79 all resident and all still returned by all(). It cost me two dead harness runs before I noticed I was tracking invisible pieces; in the app it is 32 orphaned Object3Ds per staged position, walked by every traverse and updated by the main loop forever.

history.gap: none — 3/3 demo lines verified as real checkmate with zero legal replies

The play camera crops White's own back rank off the bottom of the frame — all eight rank-1 square centres sit 20-23 px below the canvas edge, leaving a 22-28 px sliver, so clicking where your own knight or king appears to be does nothing. Deterministic at every window size, and it hits on move 2.

You cannot tell what any piece is by looking at it. Every piece is the same pale armoured figure from behind and only height separates the types: rook 119.2 px, knight 132.2 px, bishop 141.1 px on screen — 13.0 px and 8.8 px apart, 7-11 percent of their own height, with no colour, crest or marking to help. It survives at full capture resolution, so it is not the software renderer. I picked all nine of my moves by reading the FEN out of the JS console; and since the HUD never prints state.lastMove, you also cannot tell what the engine just played.

The 32 carved pieces. They are 354,599 of the 404,665 triangles the phone submits every frame (87.6%), 56 of its 117 draw calls, and 1,065 ms of a 1,919 ms frame (55%) — measured by hiding exactly those 32 groups at a fixed 800x370 buffer and timing with a readPixels fence: 1,919 -> 854 ms, 117 -> 61 calls, 404,665 -> 50,066 triangles. The board, which this round rebuilt, is now 5 calls, 11,746 triangles and 296 ms; the chamber is 34 calls and 420 ms. src/pieces is the one module the round did not open. Every figure is uniquely carved, so nothing is instanced or merged; there is one body mesh plus one arm mesh per piece, no LOD of any kind, and a pawn 30 m away at the top of the frame carries the same ~11,000 triangles as the king a metre from the lens. 64 carved geometries are resident for the 32 men actually on the board.

The stone fragment shader on the 32 pieces. With geometry, draw calls (93), triangles (139,298) and screen coverage all held EXACTLY constant and only the piece material swapped, the frame is: shipped stone 1,717 ms / MeshStandard 1,317 / MeshLambert 1,083 / MeshBasic unlit 950 / pieces hidden 850. So of the 867 ms the pieces cost, rasterising them unlit is 100 ms (11%), lighting them over the 21 punctual lights is 133-367 ms, and the custom stone GLSL is ~400 ms ON TOP of PBR and ~767 ms over unlit — 45% of the whole frame, the single largest item left. The frame is fragment-bound and still is: through the app's own path at 0.116 / 0.189 / 0.314 Mpx it costs 850 / 1,217 / 1,767 ms, i.e. ~317 ms fixed plus 4,610 ms per megapixel, against round 4's 4,780 ms/Mpx. Cutting piece triangles 2.90x did not move that slope, because triangles were never what the slope was made of.

You cannot tell what any man on the board is. The top-down play camera that fixed the occlusion spent the one cue that was left. Projecting up to 900 vertices per mesh through the live camera at 1920x804, White's back rank draws: rook 98.8x85.5 px, knight 76.3x90.4, bishop 73.0x80.6, queen 67.4x79.9, king 71.2x86.0, pawn 80.1x76.5 — against world heights of 3.07 / 3.20 / 3.55 / 4.14 / 4.56 / 2.57 m. The ordering is not compressed, it is INVERTED: a 2.57 m pawn draws 80.1 px wide and the 4.14 m queen 67.4; the 3.20 m knight draws 90.4 px tall and the 4.56 m king 86.0. At 80 degrees of declination almost nothing of a man's height reaches the screen, so what is left is a plan-view footprint that is the same chamfered hexagon for all six types, and apparent size is set by WHERE a piece stands, not what it is. The image test says the same thing without reference to geometry: crop the eight men of rank 1 at 80x80 from refs/renders/play-critic.png, normalise each to zero mean and unit variance so exposure cannot fake a difference, and take mean absolute difference. Two men of the SAME type average 0.945 apart (RR 1.138, NN 0.875, BB 0.823) while two of DIFFERENT types average 0.819 — LESS. King against bishop is 0.533, the most similar pair on the rank; every different-type pair on the board is closer than the two rooks are to each other. The 20-px SVG glyph in the HUD tray reads instantly as a queen, a bishop, a knight. The 76-px carved model on the board does not. Nothing else on screen closes the gap: there are no rank/file coordinates anywhere (the Record panel prints 'Nxc2' and nothing tells you where c2 is), and interactive.ts never marks the engine's from/to squares — aff.setSelection / setDestinations / setCheck are the only board marks, and all three fire only for YOUR move.
